source: Written 2026-10-23/24 by Claude Sonnet from our own summaries of the NC 2017 standards, and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin.

notes.NC17.K.CC.1: Counting forward only, by ones and tens within 100. Skills: next number by ones (5), next number by tens (7), missing numbers (4), counting across a ten (4), counting up to 100 (3), starting at any number (3), patterns of tens (4).
notes.NC17.K.CC.3: Numerals cannot be drawn or traced in text, so the questions test choosing or writing the right numeral for a number word, a count told in words, and zero as none. Handwriting form (reversed digits) cannot be tested here. Counts are told in words, never shown as a picture. Kindergarten: picture work is written as symbols in a row (counted by the child) or as lists of named things. Letters-in-a-word and long lists count the whole set and stay within 20.
notes.NC17.K.CC.4: Shapes, dot cards and hands are written out in words; seeing 1-5 at a glance is tested through described dot patterns (square, triangle, 2+3 split). Numbers stay within 20 and every question is one step. Written as text: dot patterns are described by where the dots are, never pictured. Numbers stay within 20, mostly within 10; subitizing questions stay within 5.
notes.NC17.K.CC.5: Picture work is written out as rows of letters or lists of names, counted in the text. Counts stay within 20; no question asks how many more, and none chains comparisons. Counting categories (how many of one kind) is left out: it belongs to K.MD.3. Counting is shown as written lists and repeated symbols; counts are generated from arrays/rep() in scripts/build-b5-NC17.K.CC.5.mjs. No how-much-more comparisons.
notes.NC17.K.CC.6: Pictures are written out as rows of O. Kindergarten compares only (more, fewer, same), never how much more; matching questions are one step. Text only: groups are shown as lists of marks, as numbers in a story or as real-world counts (legs, wheels). No question asks how many more or fewer. Counts stay within 10, never chain two comparisons, and three-group comparisons are left out.
notes.NC17.K.CC.7: Only two written numerals are compared at a time, all within 1 to 10; no question asks how much more or less, and none chains comparisons. Comparison words are greater than, less than and equal to; the symbols are left to Grade 1. Kindergarten comparison of two written numerals to 10, text only: numerals are given in the stem. Never asks how much more; no chains of comparisons.
notes.NC17.K.OA.1: Representations (fingers, drawings, acting out) are written as short stories; everything within 10. Pictures and drawings are written as words; fingers, objects, acting out, words and expressions are all tested as text. Sums and differences stay within 10. Two difficulty-3 questions ask which item does NOT match.
notes.NC17.K.OA.2: Everything is one step and inside 10. Skills: add to (6), take from (6), put together (6), take apart / one part unknown (6), matching a story and a number sentence (6). The change-unknown and start-unknown problems are Grade 1 (OA.1), so they are left out. Objects and drawings are written as a story (blocks, circles Zoe draws).
notes.NC17.K.OA.3: Zero is left out as a part (Kindergarten pairs here use 1 or more in each part). Drawings are replaced by number sentences and short stories. Order of a pair (3 and 4 versus 4 and 3) is never asked, since it is ambiguous at this age.
notes.NC17.K.OA.4: Written for Kindergarten: one step, numbers 0 to 10, ten-frames and objects described in words. Skills: story 7, number sentence 4 (+ missing start 3), ten-frame 3, pairs 6, zero and ten 3.
notes.NC17.K.OA.6: Total up to 5, one step. "Without counting one by one" (subitizing) cannot be tested in text, so groups are written as numbers and the questions test combining small groups and their partners.
notes.NC17.K.OA.5: Kept to sums and differences within 5, one step, no missing-number sentences (those come in Grade 1). Pictures are told in words.
notes.NC17.K.NBT.1: All pictures (ten frames, strips, bundles) are described in words. No question asks how much more; compare questions ask only who has more.
notes.NC17.K.MD.1: Words only, so the questions ask which words and things are measurable and which attribute a word tells about (length, height, weight). No comparing and no "how much more" (that is K.MD.2). 9 of 30 are numeric because only counting questions ("how many of these words...") fit a number answer; the rest are choice. Skills: tell what can be measured (6), match a word to its attribute (6), choose what to measure (7), name several attributes of one object (7), pick an object that has an attribute (4).
notes.NC17.K.MD.2: Kindergarten compares two objects directly and never asks how much more, so every question asks which one, or counts objects against one reference object (each compared directly, never chained). Pictures are written out in words; numeric questions are counts or a typed object number (1 or 2). Only length, height and weight are used, with line-up-the-ends and the attribute word.
notes.NC17.K.MD.3: Kindergarten: lists are written out as words; counts kept within 12 and no question asks how many more. Sorting is by color, shape, size or kind.
notes.NC17.K.G.1: Kindergarten: shapes and positions are given in words only. A ball is called a sphere; shapes are named, never counted by sides beyond what the standard needs. Some questions list items by name so the student must know which are spheres, cylinders, cubes or circles. No pictures.
notes.NC17.K.G.2: Kindergarten: shapes are named from sides, corners, faces or everyday things written out, since no pictures are shown. Naming is a choice skill by nature, so only 7 numeric questions are written: each counts the shapes (or things) that have one name, which needs the naming first. Names used: circle, square, triangle, rectangle, hexagon, sphere, cube, cone, cylinder. Descriptions of a square never list rectangle among the options, because a square is also a rectangle. Orientation and size appear in the turned-shape and big/small questions.
notes.NC17.K.G.3: Only flat-or-solid is tested (naming shapes and their attributes belong to other standards). Pictures are written out, so everyday objects (ball, box, can) stand for solid shapes and a drawing on paper for a flat one. A few numeric questions give the position in a written list.
notes.NC17.K.G.4: Thirty questions in words only (no pictures): same shape in different sizes and turns, flat against solid, corners and sides, and sorting short lists. Comparisons are never "how many more".
notes.NC17.K.G.5: Text-only: building and drawing are asked through sides and corners of the shape being made, solids by what they are modeled on. Drawing itself (the act) cannot be shown, so the draw questions ask what the finished shape must have. No "how many more" comparisons; the "how many more sticks" ones are an unfinished build (3+?=4 style, within 10). Zero as an answer appears once (a circle has no straight sides).
notes.NC17.K.G.6: Shapes are written out in words; no pictures. Kindergarten counts stay within 10 and each question is one step.

questions.skill: Count by ones: the next number
questions.stem: Count: 4, 5, 6, ?. What number comes next?
questions.solution: Counting by ones, each number is 1 more. 6 and 1 more is 7.

solve.work: Ball and block are both solid; triangle, circle, square are flat.

questions.skill: Sort a group by an attribute
questions.stem: Here are three shapes: a circle, a square and a triangle. How many of them have corners?
questions.solution: The square has corners. The triangle has corners. The circle has none. So 2 shapes have corners.

solve.work: Square and triangle have corners; circle does not: 2.

questions.skill: Same shape, turned a different way
questions.stem: Jo turns a triangle so it points down. What shape is it now?
questions.solution: Turning a shape does not change it. It is still a triangle.

solve.work: Turning does not change the shape: still a triangle.

questions.skill: Likenesses and differences in everyday words

A ball has flat sides, but a block does not.
A block is round, but a ball is not.
A ball and a block are both round.
questions.answer: A ball is round, but a block is not.
questions.solution: A ball is round all over. A block has flat sides.

solve.answer: A ball is round, but a block is not.

questions.skill: Same shape, different size

questions.solution: They are different sizes, but both are circles.

questions.skill: Compare shapes by corners and sides

questions.solution: The square has 4 corners. The triangle has 3 corners. The square has more.

questions.skill: Sort a group by an attribute
questions.stem: Here are six shapes: a square, a hexagon, a triangle, a rectangle, a circle and a rectangle. How many of them have more than 3 corners?
questions.solution: The square has 4, the hexagon has 6 and each rectangle has 4. The triangle has 3 and the circle has none. So 4 shapes have more than 3 corners.

solve.work: More than 3 corners: square(4), hexagon(6), rectangle(4), rectangle(4) = 4. Triangle 3, circle 0.

questions.skill: Solid shapes: points and flat ends
questions.stem: A can and a cone sit on a table. Which one has a point at the top?
questions.solution: A cone comes to a point. The top of a can is flat.

solve.work: A cone sitting (on its base) has a point at the top; a can is flat on top.

questions.skill: Same shape, turned a different way
questions.stem: Which shape is the same as a rectangle that is turned on its side?
questions.solution: Turning a shape on its side does not change what shape it is.

solve.work: A turned rectangle is still a rectangle.

questions.skill: Same shape, different size

questions.solution: A square has 4 corners, big or small.

questions.skill: Sort a group by an attribute
questions.stem: Here are four things: a ball, a circle, a cube and a square. How many of them have no corners?
questions.solution: The ball is round and has no corners. The circle has no corners. The cube and the square have corners. So 2 have no corners.

solve.work: Ball and circle have no corners; cube and square do: 2.

questions.skill: Flat and solid shapes compared

choices: A ball is solid, but a circle is flat.
A ball is flat, but a circle is solid.
A ball has corners, but a circle has none.
A ball and a circle are both flat.
questions.answer: A ball is solid, but a circle is flat.
questions.solution: You can hold a ball and it takes up space, so it is solid. A circle is a flat shape.

solve.answer: A ball is solid, but a circle is flat.
solve.work: A ball is solid, a circle is flat.

questions.skill: Sort a group by an attribute
questions.stem: Here are five shapes: a square, a triangle, a rectangle, a circle and a square. How many of them have 4 sides?
questions.solution: Each square has 4 sides and the rectangle has 4 sides. The triangle has 3 and the circle has none that are straight. So 3 shapes have 4 sides.

questions.skill: Sides and corners go together
questions.stem: A flat shape has 3 corners. How many sides does it have?
questions.solution: A flat shape with 3 corners is a triangle. A triangle has 3 sides.

solve.work: A flat shape with 3 corners is a triangle: 3 sides.

questions.skill: Say how two shapes are alike
questions.stem: Which sentence tells how a triangle and a square are alike?
choices: Both have only 3 sides and 3 corners
Both have only 4 sides and 4 corners
Both have corners and straight sides
Both have a curved side and no corners
questions.answer: Both have corners and straight sides
questions.solution: A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. A square has 4 straight sides and 4 corners. They are alike because both have corners and straight sides. They do not have the same number of sides, and neither one is curved.

solve.answer: Both have corners and straight sides
solve.work: Triangle has 3 sides/3 corners, square 4/4; both have corners and straight sides; neither has curved sides.

questions.skill: Compare shapes by corners and sides
questions.stem: A triangle and a rectangle sit side by side. Which sentence is true?
choices: They have the same number of corners.
questions.solution: A triangle has 3 corners. A rectangle has 4 corners. The rectangle has more.

solve.work: Rectangle 4 corners, triangle 3: rectangle has more.

questions.skill: Sort a group by an attribute
questions.stem: Here are five shapes: a circle, a square, a triangle, a circle and a rectangle. How many of them have no corners?
questions.solution: The square, the triangle and the rectangle have corners. The two circles have none. So 2 shapes have no corners.

questions.skill: Same shape, turned a different way

questions.solution: Laying a solid shape on its side does not change what shape it is. It is still a cone.

questions.skill: Same shape, different size

questions.solution: Size does not change the shape. Both have 4 sides and 4 corners, so both are squares.

solve.work: Different sizes, same shape: she is wrong, both are squares.

questions.skill: Flat and solid shapes compared

choices: A cube is flat, but a square is solid.
A cube is solid, but a square is flat.
A cube has no corners, but a square has 4.
A cube is round, but a square is not.
questions.answer: A cube is solid, but a square is flat.
questions.solution: A cube is a solid shape you can hold. A square is a flat shape.

solve.answer: A cube is solid, but a square is flat.
solve.work: A cube is solid, a square is flat.

questions.skill: Compare shapes by corners and sides

questions.solution: A square has 4 corners and a rectangle has 4 corners. The other pairs have different numbers.

questions.solution: A hexagon is a flat shape with 6 straight sides. It has more sides than a square, which has 4.

questions.skill: Sort a group by an attribute

questions.solution: The cube, the square and the triangle have corners. The balls and the circle do not. So 3 shapes go in the pile.

solve.work: With corners: cube, square, triangle = 3; balls and circle have none.

questions.skill: Likenesses and differences in everyday words

solve.work: Ball and circle are both round; ball is not flat.

questions.skill: Solid shapes: points and flat ends

questions.solution: A can has two flat round ends. A cone has one flat round end. A ball has none and a cube has flat square ends.

solve.work: A can has flat round ends; a cone has one flat round end. Cube has square faces, ball none.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

questions.solution: A shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners is a triangle.

questions.solution: A party hat is round at the bottom and has a point at the top. That is a cone.

solve.work: A party hat is shaped like a cone.

questions.skill: Tell flat shapes from solid shapes
questions.stem: Which one is a solid shape?
questions.solution: A sphere is solid, like a ball. You can hold it. A circle, a square and a triangle are flat.

solve.work: Triangle, square, circle are flat; a sphere is solid.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

questions.solution: A triangle has 3 corners.

questions.solution: A square has 4 sides. Max uses 4 straws.

solve.work: A square has 4 sides; 1 straw each, 4 straws.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces

questions.solution: A triangle has 3 sides. Tia uses 3 sticks.

questions.skill: Tell flat shapes from solid shapes

questions.solution: The circle and the triangle are flat. The cube is solid. So 2 shapes are flat.

solve.work: Circle and triangle are flat; the cube is solid. 2.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces
questions.stem: A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides. Tom builds one with sticks, 1 stick for each side. How many long sticks does he use?
questions.solution: The rectangle has 2 long sides, so Tom uses 2 long sticks.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners
questions.stem: Mia draws a shape with no straight sides and no corners. Which shape did Mia draw?
questions.solution: A circle is round. It has no straight sides and no corners.

solve.work: No straight sides, no corners: circle.

questions.skill: Name the shape that models a real object
questions.stem: Ben rolls a die. Which solid shape can Ben use to model the die?
questions.solution: A die has flat square sides and square corners all around. That is a cube.

questions.skill: Tell flat shapes from solid shapes
questions.stem: Which one is a flat shape?
questions.solution: A square is flat. A cube, a cone and a sphere are solid shapes.

solve.work: Square is 2-D; cube, cone, sphere are solids.

questions.skill: Build a solid shape
questions.stem: Lena builds a solid shape with clay. It has a flat round bottom and a point at the top. Which shape is it?
questions.solution: A solid shape with a round bottom and a point at the top is a cone. A cylinder has two flat round ends.

solve.work: Flat round base and a point on top: cone.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

questions.solution: A shape with 6 straight sides and 6 corners is a hexagon.

questions.skill: Build a solid shape

questions.solution: Jen uses 1 cube and 1 cone. That makes 2 solid shapes.

solve.work: A cube and a cone: 2 solid shapes.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces

questions.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides. Pia uses 6 straws.

solve.work: A hexagon has 6 sides, so 6 straws.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces
questions.stem: Kim has 3 sticks. She joins them end to end. Which flat shape can she build?
questions.solution: Three sticks make 3 sides. A flat shape with 3 sides is a triangle.

solve.work: Three sticks joined end to end close into a triangle; square/rectangle need 4, circle none.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces
questions.stem: Vic is building a triangle with sticks. He has put down 2 sticks. How many more sticks does he need?
questions.solution: A triangle needs 3 sticks. Vic has 2. He needs 1 more stick, because 2 and 1 make 3.

solve.work: A triangle has 3 sides; 3 - 2 = 1 more stick.

questions.skill: Name the shape that models a real object
questions.stem: A door is flat. It has 2 long sides, 2 short sides and 4 square corners. Which flat shape can Eli draw to model the door?
questions.solution: A flat shape with 2 long sides, 2 short sides and 4 square corners is a rectangle. A square has 4 sides that are all the same length.

solve.work: 2 long, 2 short sides, 4 square corners: rectangle.

questions.skill: Name the shape that models a real object
questions.stem: Which object can Rosa model with a cylinder?
questions.solution: A soup can has two flat round ends and a curved side. That is a cylinder. A ball is a sphere, a party hat is a cone and a die is a cube.

solve.work: A soup can is a cylinder; ball sphere, party hat cone, die cube.

questions.skill: Build a solid shape
questions.stem: Pam rolls clay in her hands to make a ball. Which solid shape did she make?
questions.solution: A ball is round all over, with no flat sides. That solid shape is a sphere.

solve.work: A rolled ball is a sphere.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces
questions.stem: Wes is building a rectangle with sticks. He has put down 2 long sticks and 1 short stick. How many more sticks does he need?
questions.solution: A rectangle needs 2 long sticks and 2 short sticks. Wes has both long sticks and 1 short stick. He needs 1 more short stick.

solve.work: A rectangle needs 4 sticks (2 long, 2 short). He has 3, so 1 more (a short one).

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

choices: Draw 3 straight sides that meet at 3 corners
Draw 4 straight sides that meet at 4 corners
Draw 1 round line that has no corners
Draw 3 round lines that meet at 3 corners
questions.answer: Draw 3 straight sides that meet at 3 corners
questions.solution: A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. The other directions make a different shape or a shape that cannot close.

solve.answer: Draw 3 straight sides that meet at 3 corners
solve.work: A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.

questions.skill: Tell flat shapes from solid shapes

choices: It is a solid shape that can roll
It is a flat shape with 3 corners
It is a flat shape with 4 straight sides
It is a solid shape with a point at the top
questions.answer: It is a flat shape with 4 straight sides
questions.solution: A square is a flat shape. It has 4 straight sides and 4 corners. It cannot roll and it has no point like a cone.

solve.answer: It is a flat shape with 4 straight sides
solve.work: A square is a flat shape with 4 straight sides.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

questions.solution: The straight sides meet at the corners. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it has 6 corners.

solve.work: A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 corners.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

questions.solution: A flat shape with 2 long sides and 2 short sides is a rectangle. It has 4 corners.

questions.skill: Name the shape that models a real object
questions.stem: Dan cuts a square sandwich from one corner to the opposite corner. Each half has 3 straight sides. Which flat shape does each half model?
questions.solution: Each half has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. That is a triangle.

solve.work: Each half has 3 straight sides: a triangle.

questions.skill: Draw a flat shape from its sides and corners

questions.solution: A circle is round. It has no straight sides, so the answer is 0.

questions.skill: Name the shape that models a real object

solve.work: A book cover is a rectangle; a plate is a circle, pizza slice roughly a triangle, basketball a sphere.

questions.skill: Build a solid shape
questions.stem: Lena wants to build a tower shaped like a cylinder. Which blocks should she stack, one on top of another?
questions.solution: A cylinder has round flat ends and a curved side. Stacking flat round blocks makes that shape.

solve.work: A cylinder is a stack of flat circles: flat round blocks.

questions.skill: Build a flat shape from sticks and count the pieces
questions.stem: Pam is building a hexagon with sticks. She has put down 4 sticks. How many more sticks does she need?
questions.solution: A hexagon needs 6 sticks. Pam has 4. She needs 2 more sticks, because 4 and 2 make 6.

solve.work: A hexagon has 6 sides: 6 - 4 = 2 more sticks.

questions.skill: Join two shapes into one new shape
questions.stem: Mia puts 2 same squares side by side. Their sides touch and there are no gaps. What long shape do they make?
questions.solution: Two squares side by side make a shape that is longer than it is tall. It has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners, so it is a rectangle.

solve.work: Two equal squares joined side to side make a shape twice as long as it is tall: a rectangle, not a square.

questions.skill: Join two shapes into one new shape
questions.stem: Cut a circle in half. You get 2 half circles. Put the 2 halves back together. What shape do you make?
questions.solution: The two halves fit back together to make the round shape they came from: a circle.

solve.work: Two halves of a circle put back together make the whole circle.

questions.skill: Join two shapes into one new shape
questions.stem: Cut a square from one corner to the opposite corner. You get 2 triangles. Put the 2 triangles together the same way. What shape do you get?
questions.solution: The 2 triangles fit back together along the cut. They make the square they were cut from.

solve.work: A square cut on its diagonal gives 2 triangles; joined back along the cut they make the square again.

questions.skill: Join many shapes into a larger shape
questions.stem: Jo glues 3 paper squares in a row. The squares are the same and touch side to side. What shape is the banner?
questions.solution: Three squares in a row make a long shape with 4 straight sides and 4 square corners. It is a rectangle.

solve.work: Three equal squares in a row make a long shape with 4 square corners: a rectangle.

questions.skill: Join two shapes into one new shape
questions.stem: Ana puts a triangle on top of a square. The bottom side of the triangle is as long as the top of the square. What does it look like?
questions.solution: The square is the walls and the triangle is the pointed roof, so the shapes together look like a house.

solve.work: A triangle sitting on a square with matching sides looks like a house with a pointed roof.

questions.skill: Take a larger shape apart
questions.stem: A long rectangle is made from squares in a row. It has 3 squares. Jo takes it apart into squares. How many squares does Jo have?
questions.solution: Taking the rectangle apart gives back the 3 squares it was made from.

solve.work: 3 squares in the rectangle, taken apart gives 3 squares.

questions.skill: Pieces needed to finish a larger shape

questions.solution: One square is made from 2 triangles, so she uses 2.

questions.skill: Count the squares in rows of a larger shape

questions.solution: Count 2 in the first row and 2 in the second row: 2 + 2 = 4.

questions.skill: Count the pieces used in several larger shapes

questions.solution: 1 square and 1 triangle make 2 shapes.

questions.skill: Add pieces to a larger shape

questions.solution: 2 squares and 1 more square make 3 squares.

solve.work: 2 by 2 equal squares make a shape as tall as it is wide: a big square.

questions.skill: Join many shapes into a larger shape

questions.solution: A shape with 6 straight sides is a hexagon. Six triangles around a point make one.

solve.work: Six equilateral triangles around a point form a 6-sided shape: a hexagon.

questions.skill: Choose the pieces for a larger shape

questions.solution: Each half circle is half of a circle. Put two halves together and they make a whole circle. Squares and triangles have straight sides and cannot make a round shape.

solve.work: Two half circles join to make a circle; the other pairs have straight sides.

questions.skill: Choose the pieces for a larger shape
questions.stem: Ben wants to make a shape like a house, with a flat bottom and a pointed roof. Which two shapes should he put together?
questions.solution: The square makes the walls and the triangle makes the pointed roof. A circle would make a round top, and two squares would make a long rectangle.

solve.work: A square for the flat-bottomed body and a triangle for the pointed roof.

questions.skill: Join two shapes into one new shape

choices: A door with a round top
A house with a pointed roof

questions.solution: The rectangle is the door and the half circle is its round top.

solve.answer: A door with a round top
solve.work: A rectangle with a half circle on top looks like a door with a round top (arched door).

questions.solution: The first row has 3 squares and the second row has 3 squares: 3 + 3 = 6.

questions.solution: One circle needs 2 half circles. Two circles need 2 + 2 = 4 half circles.

questions.solution: Each house uses 2 shapes. For 3 houses: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 shapes.

questions.solution: She needs 6 and has 4. Count up from 4 to 6: that is 2 more.

questions.skill: Add pieces to a larger shape

questions.solution: 4 squares and 2 more squares make 4 + 2 = 6 squares.

questions.skill: Choose the pieces for a larger shape

solve.work: Six equilateral triangles around a point make a hexagon (6 sides). 2 squares make a 4-sided rectangle; circles and half circles have curved sides.

questions.skill: Choose the pieces for a larger shape
questions.stem: Mara wants to make a big square. She has only the pieces named below. Which pieces can she use?
choices: 4 same squares, 2 on top and 2 on the bottom

solve.work: The same 4 squares are just moved, so he used 4 squares both times.

solve.work: Cutting a square corner to corner gives 2 triangles.

solve.work: Body 1 rectangle; top 1 triangle; 2 side triangles: 1 rectangle and 1+2 = 3 triangles.
